cells.tense: You're here, tending something you can't fully see yet.
cells.verb: keeping what's growing alive with steady, practical care
cells.place: in the stretch where there's only enough light for the next step
cells.ask: If you want it: let one person see what this quiet tending has cost you, and when one piece of it is finished, set it down as done rather than carrying it on. Care that doesn't wear you out comes back from that.
cells.core:
You're here, tending something you can't fully see yet. You don't know what it turns into, and you're not forcing it to tell you — you water what's in front of you, keep two things going at once, and take the next step when it shows. That's rarer than it sounds: most people either demand the whole road or stop walking. You're doing neither.

None of this is visible from outside, which is fine, except that it costs you something and no one's counting it. You might let one person see the cost. And the pieces that have finished — you're allowed to put them down.
cells.sheetLine: You tend what you can't see the end of, and you don't force it.

cells.tense: You're already tending a future that hasn't shown up yet.
cells.verb: managing every possible branch of what might grow
cells.place: in the stretch where there's only enough light for the next step
cells.ask: Try this instead: take one thing you already imagined that actually came true, and sit with it as finished — feel it done, without planning what it should become next. The holding gets lighter when it isn't clutching.
cells.core:
You're already tending a future that hasn't shown up yet. The not-knowing is uncomfortable, so you're trying to care for all of it at once — budgeting for roads you can't see, pruning branches that haven't grown, keeping every option fed in case it's the one. It looks like responsibility. It's exhaustion wearing responsibility's clothes.

The tending itself isn't the problem; it's the reach. You're spending care on versions that may never arrive, while the things that did arrive go unenjoyed. One of them came true. You could let that one be enough for an evening.
cells.sheetLine: You're caring for outcomes that don't exist yet, and it's wearing you out.

cells.tense: Somewhere back there, you stopped tending because you couldn't see where it was going.
cells.place: in the stretch where there's only enough light for the next step
cells.ask: Don't force the tending back. Instead, find the one thing you still want even though it's unclear, and carry that wanting one more week without needing to know how it ends. Care comes back behind hope, not ahead of it.
cells.core:
Somewhere back there, you stopped tending because you couldn't see where it was going. The fog didn't lift, so the watering stopped, and now there's something half-grown that you're neither killing nor keeping. You're still standing at that door, deciding whether the not-knowing was a reason to leave.

It wasn't, but telling yourself to go back and care harder won't do it either. What's gone quiet isn't the care — it's the hope the care was running on. Find the one thing you still want anyway, under the uncertainty. Carry that first. The hands follow.
cells.sheetLine: You let it go unwatered because you couldn't see the end.

cells.tense: You're already the one keeping this alive, and you call it waiting to see.
cells.verb: quietly feeding both sides of an undecided thing
cells.place: in the stretch where there's only enough light for the next step
cells.ask: Say it plainly to one person: what you've been keeping alive on purpose, and what it's costing you to do it. Once it's said, the holding stops being a secret clutch and becomes a choice you can set down when it's done.
cells.core:
You're already the one keeping this alive, and you call it waiting to see. Every day you make small practical choices that keep an uncertain thing going — attention here, a door held open there, two needs fed when one would be easier. Then you describe yourself as undecided, as if the thing were surviving on its own.

It isn't. It's surviving because you tend it, and the cost of that tending lands on you whether you claim it or not. The care is real work. The simplest fix is to say so, out loud, to someone — what you're keeping alive and why. Then it's yours, and yours to hold lightly.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping it alive on purpose. You're just not saying so.
